analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic refuge and offshore waters to oil and gas drilling while weakening environmental review.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2009 with 50 Republican cosponsors, the bill was referred to four House committees and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, pitched as a stimulus that costs taxpayers nothing, would have opened the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain and every offshore planning area with commercial interest to oil and gas leasing, and made oil shale and tar sands lease sales mandatory where states show interest. It would have capped environmental impact statements at 270 days — with projects automatically approved if the review runs late — stripped carbon dioxide out of the Clean Air Act, barred states from getting waivers to set their own greenhouse-gas car rules, and sped up nuclear plant licensing by cutting public hearing requirements. It also would have routed all challenges to federal energy leasing into a single Washington, D.C. court with tight deadlines.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies, which would gain access to the Arctic refuge coastal plain, mandatory offshore lease sales, and shortened legal and environmental review. Nuclear plant developers, oil shale and tar sands developers, and automakers (who would avoid stricter state emissions rules) also gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies, nuclear developers, automakers

how_it_helps.text: It would open the 1002 Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil and gas leasing, requiring a first lease sale of at least 200,000 acres within 22 months of enactment and repealing the 1980 law that keeps the area closed.

It would deem the draft 2010-2015 Outer Continental Shelf oil and gas leasing program approved and its environmental impact statement complete without further review, and require lease sales in every offshore planning area with commercial interest.
It would require environmental impact statements to be finished within 270 days, and if not, the project would be automatically deemed to have no significant environmental impact.

It would declare that carbon dioxide, methane from agriculture or livestock, and water vapor are not air pollutants under the Clean Air Act, and bar the EPA from granting any state a waiver to regulate vehicle greenhouse-gas emissions.
It would repeal the 30-day public notice requirement before hearings on nuclear power plant construction permits.
It would let state governors suspend Endangered Species Act protections during declared emergencies and bar consideration of greenhouse-gas impacts on any species under the Act.

It would route all legal challenges to federal energy leasing decisions into the D.C. federal district court, which would have to resolve cases within 180 days or see them dismissed with prejudice, with appeal only to the Supreme Court.

It would send 50 percent of leasing revenues to Alaska, create a local impact aid fund capped at $11 million for North Slope communities, and extend coastal states' seaward boundaries from three to 12 nautical miles.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the environmental and climate costs: drilling in a pristine refuge and expanded offshore leasing carry spill and habitat risks, weakened environmental review makes hasty federal decisions harder to challenge, and excluding carbon dioxide from the Clean Air Act removes a tool for limiting climate change. Federal taxpayers also forgo the chance to secure higher royalties through normal competitive review.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through environmental and climate risk

drawbacks.text: Opening the Arctic refuge coastal plain to drilling, even with the bill's protective stipulations and 2,000-acre surface footprint cap, carries oil-spill and habitat risks in one of the country's most intact wild areas — a cost its supporters had to acknowledge.

The 270-day environmental review deadline with automatic approval on delay, the 20-day public comment window for the refuge's review, and the rule that courts must presume the government's environmental analysis correct unless disproven by clear and convincing evidence would sharply limit the public's ability to scrutinize federal energy decisions.
Removing carbon dioxide from the Clean Air Act and barring states from setting their own vehicle greenhouse-gas standards would prevent climate regulation through the main existing legal channels.
Any new oil from the refuge or offshore areas would take years to reach market, so the bill's promise of near-term stimulus and price relief was uncertain even on its own terms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits — royalty revenue, potential jobs, and long-run energy supply — would flow mostly to the companies that lease the land, while its costs fall on the public: weakened environmental review, stripped-back climate and species protections, and drilling in the Arctic refuge. Even a supporter who accepts drilling in principle would have to concede that the litigation and review limits go well beyond what a carefully designed leasing program needs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and several subcommittees in 2009, none of which ever scheduled it for a markup or a floor vote, and it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Rob Bishop of Utah introduced the bill on March 11, 2009, with 27 original Republican cosponsors, and 50 Republicans in total signed on.
The Speaker sent it to four committees at once — Natural Resources, Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, and Science and Technology — which meant each had to act before the bill could move.
It was referred to subcommittees in March and August 2009, and no committee or subcommittee ever took it up for a markup or vote.
The bill never received a floor vote in the House or Senate and expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the Arctic refuge stayed closed to drilling and the Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Environmental Policy Act remained unchanged — so the public kept existing environmental protections, and oil and gas companies did not gain the access this bill would have given them.

for.name: Rep. Rob Bishop
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 50 Republican cosponsors.

for.name: 50 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: Democratic chairs of the Natural Resources, Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, and Science and Technology committees
against.role: Committee chairs controlling the House agenda
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or vote in any of the four committees to which it was referred; it sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 50 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic majority that controlled the committees never moved the bill; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would hand them access to the Arctic refuge coastal plain and mandatory offshore lease sales while cutting the environmental review and litigation they face; the spill, habitat, and climate risks of that access fall on the public rather than on the lessees.

industries.industry: Oil shale and tar sands developers
industries.note: It would convert discretionary oil shale lease sales into mandatory ones held every 270 days in any state showing interest, opening public land to unconventional fuel development with less review.

It would repeal the 30-day public notice before construction-permit hearings, reducing public participation in licensing new plants; the industry gains speed while the public gives up a notice safeguard.
By barring EPA waivers for state greenhouse-gas vehicle rules, it would spare automakers stricter emissions standards that consumers otherwise benefit from through lower fuel use.
The bill authorizes commercial lease sales of federal offshore resources for renewable energy production and mariculture, a small opening that could benefit offshore wind and ocean farming.
